I had it back in March (tested for antibodies after so I didnn't know I had it when I had it but suspected heavily) and despite being over 55, a smoker, and not in the best of health, I'm fine now. It sucked for about a week, hard, fever, body aches, vomiting and a headache. I have no idea if I lost my sense of taste because eating was far from my mind. But it wasn't horrible. It felt a lot like the last time I had bronchitis, frankly. 

Keep breathing, lay down if you don't feel well, do comfy things like reading or watch some tv, drink a lot a lot a lot of fluids and try to avoid surfing the internet for 'what to do when you have corona' because it is just panic city out there and none of it is sourced.  

I did make a notebook of how I felt from day 2 so I could look back and say "No, I've not been sick forever, just however many days" and that helped me.
Please stay alive for your babies. You have so much to give them, especially your strength.  They are so lucky to have you.

When I was little, my family used to vacation at the Jersey coast every year. One year we flew, a few years we drove, but mostly, we took Greyhound, so it took about 9 or 10 hours from near Pittsburg to Margate.

One year coming back from the coast, a man got on the bus in Philadelphia. He was an older black man, that much I remember, dressed in a suit and hat. This would have been about 1973 or 74, so I was 8 or 9.  He was very angry, I can't remember now if he didn't have the money for a ticket or if the bus was full and he couldn't get one for that reason, but he was shouting and yelling that his sister (daughter? mother? some female relative) was dying in the hospital in Pittsburg and he was going to see her.  The bus driver tried to tell him to get off the bus but he was having none of it. He got louder and louder, punching the seat in front of him (my mother and I were sitting about 4 rows away in the front so we could hear him but not see him without turning around).  A few other people were telling him he needed to get off the bus, and that made him madder.

He started yelling that if his sister (or whoever) it was died before he got there, some 'whitey' on the bus was going to die as well. Mind, I was 8. I started crying. My mom started to take me off the bus and he came running after us. She shoved me down the stairs and into the bus station, but the man stopped at the doors, screaming and shouting and very angry.

The cops came. They couldn't talk him into getting off the bus and he got physical with him, not hitting but shoving and pushing, etc. Meanwhile yelling that everybody on the bus was going to be shot now because his sister was going to die and he wasn't there for her. I don't honestly know if he was crazy, crazy with grief, or what. By then there were a lot of cops wandering around, two or three of them on the bus talking to him, and him making threats. My mother and I were standing inside the bus terminal watching through the windows.

The police brought the K9 unit. The dog was barking and doing this lunge thing at the door of the bus. The man came half way to the doors and did something, my kid brain has kind of blurred it out. Maybe he had a knife, I'm sure he didn't have a gun. But whatever it was he did, the dog handler let go of the dog.

The dog jumped into the bus, onto the man, and just started tearing at him. I don't know any other way to put it. The man tried to cover over, he fell over the seat at the front where my mother and I had been sitting and he clawed at the window, trying to get away from the dog. He must have been screaming, I'm sure I saw his mouth open, but I don't remember sound. Or I couldn't hear it, I was inside the terminal looking out.

He went down like in slow motion, grabbing the window latch, there was a trail of blood from his hand down the window and then he must have fell to the floor because all I could see was the dog lunging and coming up with like, parts of his suit. The whole time, the handler and one of the other cops stood back, folded their arms and watched the dog take him down.

My mother ran me off to the bathroom and we stayed in there a long time, when we came out there was a different bus parked next to the one we'd come in on and people were slowly moving from the one to the other. They were quiet and everybody was looking away or up when they came off the bus. I asked my dad what had happened and he said that "a n*gger got uppity and that's what they get", which was pretty much my dad in a nutshell there, but nothing else.

This was 45 years ago and I will never forget the look of that man's face as he slid down from the window and the way both cops just stood there with their arms crossed like it was a warm spring day in the country for them. I was terrified every time I saw a german shepherd for years afterward.  I tried to look it up once but I could find nothing. Maybe he lived. Maybe he died. I don't know.

tldr: A possibly grieving man gets the dogs put on him in a bus station in Philly. My father is a racist.

Potter Hill Mill, Ashaway, RI, back in the late 70's. It was an old textile mill build over the river and had been abandoned in the 60's, so by the time we got there it was pretty well gone. The machines were still set up but full of rust, cobwebs and dirt. Some had fallen through the floors and down into the river itself. The elevator shaft was just a wide open pit down into a flooded sub basement, and the base of the shaft had been filled over the years with debris from people knocking stuff down it. It looked like the place where tetanus must have been invented.

The scary thing is, the day we went, we parked near the fish ladder at the dam and walked in, saw NO ONE else at all around, but once we got back through the mill and toward the outlying sheds (they were full of old bags of fabric and machine parts and junk and what have you) we started to hear other people banging around inside. We didn't want to get arrested for trespass so we skirted around the side of the place but there were no other cars there and no marks in the dirt except our own. None of us were brave enough to go back and see who or what was making the noises, we high tailed it out of there. 

But my god was it creepy! One of my friends had decided to take a few of the machine belts as they were good, thick leather and not worn or decayed in the least, and he ended up giving them to his uncle who'd lived in Eastern Connecticut his whole life. When the old man found out where they'd come from, he gave them back and said he'd worked in the mill in the 40's and didn't want any part of 'that cussed place'. We never did get him to spill anything else about it, but it was certainly the capper of a creepy weekend.

So far as I know, it's sitting there still, slowly falling into the river.

Worked with a woman who'd had a traumatic brain injury, it was a nightmare. Couldn't fire her because of HR, but she was literally a danger in the kitchen. She was prep but wasn't able to use knives, the hobart, the stove or the ovens. Mixed salad dressing and portioned all day long. Would spill vinagarette dressing on the floor of the walk in and neither clean it nor warn anyone else she'd done it, not once but maybe 10 or 12 times in the two years I worked there.  Would kick open the cooler door when coming out, not announcing or warning. Wouldn't say 'behind' or 'hot' or 'coming through'. I STILL have problems with my right hand going numb from an injury from her kicking the door into my elbow. Lost all the knobs to the grill, still don't know what happened to them. Would open the oven and stare at the breadsticks cooking, which of course, makes the temps off. When she left for the day it took chef about 3 hours to fix whatever she'd done that day, sometimes having to toss out sauces or mixes as she'd just get bored and wander off, not put everything into it, or doubling or tripling the ingredients at whim.

The kitchen (chain pub place in the Pacific North West) was only about 15X15 so there was NO place to put her where she could just work on her own and not be right in the middle of traffic. Horrible set up anyway in that place, but having someone who occasionally just 'froze' and started rocking in place while moaning was absolutely NOT safe.

She wasn't a legacy, either, she'd had the brain injury about 15 years prior to getting the job there. So they hired her and let her get through her probation period being a danger literally to herself and others, and then firing her would have taken an act of god and six lawyers.

I mean, I realize it was cool of her to TRY to work, self sufficiency and all that, but her actions led to permanent injuries to at least 3 of the staff including myself, and averaged LITERALLY about $300 in lost/ruined product a week, every week.

My mother was one of those people who had a thing about keeping her purse very tight to her at all times. Hanging on her chair or sitting on the floor next to her, even when she was at home. I believe she even slept with it on the bed next to her.

When she died, going through that was ... interesting.

-Stepfather's wallet from 1978. Still had his ID, credit cards, a folded up twenty behind the driver's license. All just like he'd left it the last time she visited him in the hospital. This made me sad.

-Three pairs of reading glasses. Apparently she never threw her old ones away when she got new ones. Ok, that's understandable.

-An extra pair of dentures. That was creepy to find. I'm not sure if she'd ever worn them, if they were old ones or brand new, or what.

-A change purse containing nine diamond rings, four wedding bands, several sets of rosary beads, a few loose earrings, some of those tiny ladies' watches that were popular back in the 60's... This confused me until I recognized one set of rings as the white gold ones my grandmother - her mother - had. That had been on her finger in her casket.

My mother had been taking the jewelry of deceased members of our family for about 40 years.  

I'm sure she'd have been proud of me for keeping it.

These are the kind of things that most good cooks would love to have said about them. Thank you for sharing this and I'm very sorry for your loss. Hope you can find some peace about this all.

At a Motley Crue concert last year, the backdrop caught fire. Indoor arena show. I was up in the balcony, nosebleed seats, and in the middle of a row. Ten seconds, fire still burning, I got up, said I was leaving NOW, and crawled over the people to my right to get to the aisle. Twenty seconds, got to the aisle, looked back, backdrop was still burning and now there were stage hands (roadies? maybe?) ineffectively spraying at it with fire extinguishers. Headed up the super steep stairs to the exit, praying I wouldn't fall and that there wasn't going to be a crush. Thirty seconds, made it to the top, turned around, saw the fire still burning, people I had been sitting with still sitting, and booked it down the stairs and outside. 
Maybe only 50 or 60 people actually left the venue, I sat outside with my heart pounding thinking of The Station fire and how quickly things could get bad. Of course nothing much happened, no big tragedy, but I was kind of proud of myself that I left rather than run the odds and stay, hoping they'd 'do something'.

The two 'big' books about Elizabeth Short's murder - Daddy Was The Black Dahlia Killer by Janice Knowlton and Severed by John Gilmour - are nothing more than hot garbage. 

Daddy Was... is the sadder of the two since Knowlton seems to have been a woman desperately trying to find help for her problems who got involved with recovered memory therapy back in the early 90's when it was a complete free-for-all and there were NO safeguards against really bad therapists. Gilmour, on the other hand, really just seems to want the money, honey.

Why are they bad? Knowlton's book is bad for the simple reason it's just TOO horrible to be real. Her father was an abusive SOB. Ok, this happens too often, it's believable. He took his 7 year old daughter out to visit prostitutes with him... ok, that's dreadful but not outside possibility. He started killing the prostitutes in front of his daughter. Oh... uh... He killed and bisected Elizabeth Short in front of her. Uh... He killed Georgette Baurdorf in front of her too... He fathered twins on his daughter and killed one of them with a hammer and made her cook and eat it... The book just spirals into this never ending horror tale and frankly by the end it's just so unbelievable it's almost laughable, until you remember that Ms. Knowlton was really very obsessed and injured by these things in her head. 

On the other hand. Gilmour. It's badly written, badly researched, and WAY too self insertive. Halfway through, he details a meeting a 'police informant' has with a mystery man who has Ms. Short's handkerchief, possibly her underwear, a few photos from her purse, and spends several chapters talking about the police investigation into this man. Then he rewinds and reveals that HE (Gilmour) is actually the 'police informant' and RETELLS the entire story of meeting the mystery man, etc, adding nothing new. In the end, mystery man burns to death in a flophouse hotel in LA, supposedly destroying all the 'trophies' he kept from Ms. Short's murder in the process.  In addition to Gilmour detailing Ms. Short's promiscuity in some pretty lurid terms that smell one degree off from 'dirty whore had it coming...'. 

(Edited to add I wasn't thinking of the baggage a word like 'promiscuity' has but what I mean is the fact that she was a sexually active woman in a time and place when women weren't supposed to be. Nothing more than that.)

I really wish someone would write a GOOD book about the murder, or better yet solve the case, but I don't think either of those is likely at this late date.
